claims.text: Partial substitution of a base-alloy element with Zr enhances glass-forming ability relative to the original composition.
A rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi-type base alloy typically has limited glass-forming ability.
The proposed base alloy tends to crystallize during rapid-quenching synthesis.
Adding Zr increases atomic-size mismatch in the base alloy.
Adding Zr enhances local chemical disorder in the base alloy.
Zr substitution increases the alloy's mixing entropy.
The increased mixing entropy and atomic-size disparity slow crystal nucleation.
The increased mixing entropy and atomic-size disparity slow crystal growth.
Slower crystal nucleation and growth widen the supercooled-liquid region.
Slower crystal nucleation and growth promote glass formation.
An optimal Zr content produces a lower crystallization-onset temperature than the Zr-free base alloy.
An optimal Zr content produces a larger supercooled-liquid region than the Zr-free base alloy.
A larger supercooled-liquid region indicates improved glass-forming ability.
The glass-forming enhancement occurs only within a limited Zr-concentration range.
Too little Zr may have a negligible effect on glass-forming ability.
Excessive Zr may induce phase separation.
Excessive Zr may produce unwanted intermetallic phases.
The optimal Zr content depends on the specific base-alloy system.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that Zr slows crystallization nucleation and growth, but the predicted signature includes a lower crystallization-onset temperature, and the falsification rule treats lowered Tx as evidence of enhancement. Under identical testing conditions, slower crystallization kinetics would not straightforwardly predict earlier crystallization; the relation among Tg, Tx, and ΔT is not supplied to resolve this tension.
